idiom_name: type predicates ('v is T') and assertion signatures ('asserts v is T')
implementation_notes: TypeScript consumes this pattern as a language feature: a user-defined type guard is a function whose return type is a type predicate (function isPort(v: unknown): v is Port) and the compiler narrows the checked value for the rest of the scope - contramap written into the type system, with the proof carried to the caller. contramap is still a higher-order function over a projection, divide is &&/every, choose is a switch over a discriminated union the compiler checks for exhaustiveness, and assertion functions (asserts v is Port) put the check on the statement path so later code needs no if. Prefer this native form when parsing untrusted input into domain types; upgrade boolean-returning rules to type predicates so the narrowed type survives.
pitfalls: A type predicate is an unchecked claim: function isPort(v: unknown): v is Port { return true } compiles and lies, so the runtime test inside must actually establish the property.

Narrowing does not survive callbacks or reassignment: inside a forEach/map callback, or after assigning the value to a mutable let in an outer scope, the compiler widens it again - capture narrowed values in consts.
Array.prototype.every is typed as a plain boolean predicate and discards narrowing; filter(isPort) uses the type-predicate overload and keeps the narrowed element type instead.

variants.name: zod schemas with refinements (declarative, accumulating)
variants.idiom_name: z.object + .refine/.superRefine + safeParse; z.infer for the narrowed type
variants.implementation_notes: zod makes the schema the validator: z.object({...}) is the product combination of field schemas, .refine/.superRefine attach reusable checks to a schema (superRefine can add several issues with explicit paths), and .safeParse returns a discriminated result carrying every issue - the accumulating verdict - while z.infer derives the narrowed static type from the same declaration. Rules stay reusable because a schema is a value: compose with .and/.or/.extend/.transform and share subschemas across endpoints. Choose it at JSON/HTTP/CLI boundaries where the wire shape, the checks and the error report must come from one declaration; keep native type guards for in-process narrowing with no runtime schema.
pitfalls: .refine runs after the base type has parsed and its return value replaces the data: a refinement that silently transforms instead of rejecting hides the failure - reject with false or ctx.addIssue.
.superRefine issue paths are manual: an issue added without path reports on the object root, so clients cannot map the error back to a field.

Refinement chains are type-erased at API boundaries: z.ZodType<T> drops schema-specific methods, so a function accepting ZodType<T> cannot be extended later without re-declaring the concrete schema type.
